newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger unfazed by prospect of longer talks.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger unfazed by prospect of longer talks.

text.p: New Zealand's caretaker Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Thursday he was not concerned if coalition talks remained unresolved by the time parliament reconvened, as New Zealand First leader Winston Peters has suggested.

Parliament is due to meet by December 13 at the latest, and Bolger's conservative National Party currently leads a caretaker government after last month's inconclusive general election. Nationalist NZ First holds the balance of power between the caretaker National party government and the main opposition Labour party, and is negotiating with both.
Peters said on Wednesday he could not forecast whether New Zealand First would isolate one prospective coalition partner by December 13.
Bolger told Radio New Zealand he had always seen the potential for such delays.

"I've adopted the approach on that that we should take the time that's necessary, and if it takes us past a particular date it takes us past that date. There is nothing that can't be arranged with commonsense between the parties," Bolger said.
"What we need to do is make certain we take the appropriate level of time to put together a strong coalition government.

"I said all the way through the campaign, and many others did, that forming the first coalition government could be a quite lengthy exercise...that's the facts of life and I think we should just calmly accept them," Bolger said.

He also said he did not expect the full NZ$563,000 parliamentary fund, set up for the coalition talks, to be spent. The parties can draw on the funds to pay consultants or researchers in researching policy proposals.
"I don't anticipate the full half million will be spent, to be perfectly honest," Bolger said.
"But there are additional costs -- we do want people to have good advice and good advisers, we do want the coalition to be built on strong foundations, not on some whimsical ideas.
"That will be a very very good investment for New Zealand's future if...parties spend some of that money to get good advice so we get a good government," he said.
